headline: Amazon makes its first profit
text: Amazon reported a net profit of $5 million for the fourth quarter of 2001, its first, on sales of more than $1 billion. For the full year it still lost $567 million on sales of $3.12 billion. The company warned that the quarterly profit should not be taken as a trend.
imageCaption: Jeff Bezos (centre) visiting the Robot Co-op

headline: Euro notes and coins in the neighbouring countries
text: On 1 January euro notes and coins went into circulation in twelve EU countries, among them Germany, France, Italy and Austria. The mark, the French franc, the lira and the schilling can be exchanged until the end of February. The euro has existed since 1999, but only for accounts and electronic payments. Switzerland keeps its franc, but Swiss travellers and shoppers across the border now meet one currency on three sides.
imageCaption: Euro banknotes and coins, which replaced national currencies on 1 January 2002

headline: Euro notes and coins arrive
text: On 1 January euro banknotes and coins went into circulation in twelve countries, replacing the mark, the franc, the lira and nine other currencies, which will cease to be legal tender by the end of February. The euro has been used on currency and bond markets since January 1999 and fell against the dollar until late 2000.
imageCaption: In the first minutes of 2002, people in Maastricht look closely at the euro notes they have just drawn from a cash machine
imageCredit: Claudio Hils / ECB (photo series commissioned by the European Central Bank, as stated by NZZ)

headline: Global Crossing goes bankrupt; telecom shares slump
text: Global Crossing, which built undersea fibre-optic cables, filed for bankruptcy in January with debts of $12.4 billion, one of the largest bankruptcies ever. Coming weeks after Enron's collapse, it deepened fears about debt and accounting at telecom companies, and WorldCom's shares fell 29% in the month.
imageCaption: Global Crossing logo

headline: WorldCom paid $199 million to cover its chief's margin loans
text: WorldCom disclosed on 7 February that, after the fall in its shares, it had paid about $198.7 million to Bank of America under its guarantee of loans to chief executive Bernard Ebbers, and had lent him another $142 million, all secured by his WorldCom shares. Ebbers used the money to meet calls on loans backed by his stock, taken out for private businesses. The same day the company felt it had to reaffirm the MCI group's 60-cent dividend.
imageCaption: Bernard Ebbers, chief executive of WorldCom

headline: Nvidia restates its accounts, and fights Microsoft over Xbox prices
text: On 29 April Nvidia announced that a review by its audit committee, begun at the request of the SEC in January, concluded that its accounts for 2000, 2001 and most of 2002 must be restated, mainly for the timing of costs. The same day it disclosed that Microsoft has taken a dispute over Xbox chip prices and volumes to binding arbitration.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/0001012870-02-002921.txt (Nvidia 10-Q/A for the quarter to April 2002, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000095016802001118/d8k.htm (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive

headline: Ebbers resigns as WorldCom's shares collapse
text: Bernard Ebbers resigned as chief executive on 30 April after the board, which had lost patience with his loans, demanded he go; John Sidgmore, former head of UUNet, replaces him. The SEC is investigating WorldCom's accounting. On 22 April Salomon Smith Barney analyst Jack Grubman, long WorldCom's biggest supporter, cut his rating to 'neutral'. The shares fell 63% in April, to below $3.
imageCaption: Bernard Ebbers, chief executive of WorldCom until 30 April 2002

headline: IBM warns, then reports a 31% profit drop
text: On 8 April IBM warned that first-quarter revenue would fall to about 18.5 billion dollars from 21 billion, as customers put off spending, and that its chip unit would lose money. The results confirmed it: earnings per share fell 31% to 68 cents. New chief executive Sam Palmisano said customers everywhere deferred technology purchases.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000051143/000100547702001549/d02-37080.txt (IBM 8-K of 2002-04-08, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000051143/000089155402002124/d02-37159.txt (IBM results release of 2002-04-17, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Sam Palmisano, IBM's chief executive

headline: Xstrata relaunches in London as Glencore's coal miner
text: Xstrata, a small Zug-based holding that the commodity trader Glencore has controlled since the 1990s, floated in London in March 2002 and used the listing to buy Glencore's Enex and Duiker coal mines in Australia and South Africa. The deal makes it the world's largest exporter of thermal coal, alongside its ferroalloys and zinc businesses. Chief executive Mick Davis, the former Billiton finance director who helped merge Billiton with BHP, and his board aim to grow it into a major diversified mining company. Glencore remains the largest shareholder and markets much of the output.
source: Xstrata plc circular of 2 February 2009, part I, https://www.rns-pdf.londonstockexchange.com/rns/6630M_-2009-2-2.pdf; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xstrata; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Davis; https://www.encyclopedia.com/books/politics-and-business-magazines/xstrata-plc (all read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Aerial view of an Xstrata base-metal mine

headline: Expo.02, the Swiss national exhibition, opens on the lakes
text: Switzerland's sixth national exhibition, Expo.02, opened on 15 May and runs until 20 October. It is spread over four 'Arteplages' built for the event on the lake shores at Biel, Murten, Neuchâtel and Yverdon-les-Bains, plus a converted gravel barge that travels between them. It was planned for 2001 and postponed by a year.
imageCaption: Expo.02 at Biel/Bienne: the 'Empire of Silence' pavilion on the lakeshore

headline: WorldCom cut to junk; scraps the MCI dividend
text: The rating agencies have cut WorldCom's debt to junk (Moody's Ba2, Standard & Poor's BB), and the company plans to draw $2.65 billion from a bank credit line while it negotiates new, secured loans. It expects to write off $15-20 billion of goodwill from past acquisitions, has replaced Arthur Andersen as auditor with KPMG, has rolled Bernard Ebbers' debts to the company into a single $408 million note, and on 21 May said it would scrap the MCI tracking stock and its dividend to save $284 million a year.

headline: WorldCom admits a $3.8 billion accounting fraud
text: WorldCom said on 25 June that it had hidden $3.8 billion of ordinary expenses over five quarters by booking them as investments, turning losses into profits; it fired finance chief Scott Sullivan and must restate its results for 2001 and 2002. The SEC charged the company with fraud the next day. Earlier in the month WorldCom announced 17,000 job cuts; it has about $30 billion of debt.
imageCaption: Bernard Ebbers, former chief executive of WorldCom, 2001

headline: Intel cuts its forecast again
text: On 6 June Intel lowered its outlook for the second quarter: revenue between 6.2 and 6.5 billion dollars instead of 6.4 to 7.0 billion, mainly because of softer than expected demand in Europe, and a gross margin of about 49% instead of 53%. Technology shares are falling with the whole market.
imageCaption: Intel's leaders Gordon Moore, Craig Barrett, Andy Grove and Paul Otellini

headline: A string of verdicts revives litigation fears
text: On 11 June a Miami jury ordered Philip Morris, Brown & Williamson and Liggett to pay 37.5 million dollars to a former smoker, John Lukacs, a member of the Engle class, and found him entitled to a share of the 145 billion dollar Engle punitive award. On 21 June a federal judge in Kansas ordered R.J. Reynolds to pay 15 million dollars in punitive damages, and the industry has lost five verdicts in a row on the West Coast. On 24 June Philip Morris shares fell 7.3% to 48.80 dollars. They had been among the best blue chips this year. At the end of May Philip Morris agreed to sell Miller Brewing to South African Breweries for 3.6 billion dollars in shares plus 2 billion of debt, keeping 36% of the new SABMiller.
imageCaption: Philip Morris advertising ;;

headline: WorldCom files for bankruptcy, the largest in U.S. history
text: WorldCom filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 21 July, the largest filing in U.S. history, overtaking Enron. Days earlier, Bernard Ebbers told a congressional committee he had nothing to hide and then refused to answer questions, citing his right not to incriminate himself. The shares are close to worthless.

headline: WorldCom's collapse caps a month of accounting scandals
text: WorldCom, brought down by an accounting scandal, filed for bankruptcy on 21 July, the largest corporate insolvency ever. Revelations of corporate fraud and fears of more restated earnings sent shares plunging; President Bush gave a stern speech on accounting scandals on 9 July, and the Dow closed below 8,000 on 23 July before a late rebound. The S&P 500 lost 8% in July to 911.62.
imageCaption: Bernard Ebbers, chief executive of WorldCom

headline: WorldCom fails: the telecom bust's biggest bankruptcy
text: WorldCom, the long-distance telephone company, filed for bankruptcy in July after an accounting scandal, following Global Crossing's bankruptcy in January. The head of the FCC told the Senate that the industry owes about a trillion dollars, much of which will never be repaid. The Nasdaq fell 9% in July to 1,328.
imageCaption: Former WorldCom chief Bernard Ebbers at the House hearing on WorldCom's accounts, with Andersen's Melvin Dick, CFO Scott Sullivan and analyst Jack Grubman, Washington, 8 July 2002

headline: Citigroup's star analyst questioned over WorldCom
text: WorldCom, whose shares and bonds Citigroup's Salomon Smith Barney helped sell and whose deals it advised on, has collapsed into bankruptcy after admitting a $3.8 billion fraud. Salomon's telecom analyst Jack Grubman, who recommended WorldCom shares until April, told Congress he saw no warning signs. New York's attorney general Eliot Spitzer is investigating conflicts of interest among Wall Street analysts, Salomon among them, and Citigroup faces lawsuits over its role in Enron's financing.
imageCaption: Citigroup Center, Manhattan

headline: Rating agencies turn negative on Credit Suisse
text: In July the credit-rating agencies put Credit Suisse Group's ratings on negative outlook. The falling stock markets are eating into the capital of its insurer Winterthur, and the group is injecting capital into Winterthur and raising hybrid capital for its insurance business.
source: Credit Suisse Group Form 20-F for 2002, filed 27 March 2003, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1159510/000104746903010549/a2104752z20-f.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/credit-suisse-group (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Credit Suisse on the Paradeplatz, Zurich

headline: Exiles reveal secret nuclear sites at Natanz and Arak
text: In August an Iranian exile opposition group made public the existence of two undeclared nuclear sites in Iran: a uranium enrichment plant at Natanz and a heavy-water facility at Arak. Iran says its programme is for electricity only. The International Atomic Energy Agency wants to inspect.
imageCaption: The Natanz nuclear site, Iran

headline: McDonald's cuts its profit forecast again
text: On 17 September McDonald's lowered its 2002 earnings forecast because sales in the US and Europe were weaker than expected in the third quarter, and it is cautious on the fourth. Chairman Jack Greenberg says the US market is 'extremely competitive' and promises better value, service and menu choice. Philip Morris, J.P. Morgan and Honeywell also cut forecasts this month. McDonald's shares lost about 26% in September.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000095013102003563/dex992.txt (press release of 17 September 2002, read 2026-10-03); http://money.cnn.com/2002/09/26/news/companies/philip_morris/index.htm (via web.archive.org, read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/mcd.json
imageCaption: The Big Mac

headline: Philip Morris slashes its profit forecast
text: On 26 September Philip Morris cut its 2002 forecast to earnings growth of 3 to 5%, against about 19% analysts expected. It blamed sharp increases in state cigarette taxes (the average state tax is up 35% since June), consumer frugality, cheap imports and a black market in untaxed and counterfeit cigarettes, against which it is spending more on promotions. The shares fell 12% after hours. Its cigarette market share dipped to 49% in July.
imageCaption: Philip Morris research building, Richmond, Virginia

headline: Iraq tensions and weak data: shares fall 11 percent
text: Weak figures on production and jobs, a gloomier outlook for profits and rising tension over Iraq sent shares down again in September. On 23 September the Nasdaq hit a six-year low and the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds sank to 3.70 percent, a 40-year low, as investors fled to safety. The S&P 500 lost 11% in the month to 815.28.
imageCaption: The trading floor of the New York Stock Exchange

headline: The Nasdaq at a six-year low
text: The Nasdaq fell 11% in September to 1,172, its lowest month-end since 1996 and 77% below the record of March 2000. Accounting scandals from Enron to WorldCom have shaken trust in company figures.
imageCaption: CNBC's morning programme broadcasting from the Nasdaq MarketSite, Times Square

headline: eBay completes its purchase of PayPal
text: eBay completed its acquisition of PayPal, an online payment service widely used by eBay buyers, for $1.4 billion on October 3. It will phase out its own payment service, Billpoint.
imageCaption: PayPal's headquarters in San Jose, California

headline: Shares hit five-year lows, then jump 9 percent
text: On 7 October the S&P 500 closed at 785.28, its lowest since 1997, and by 9 October the Dow was below 7,200 and the Nasdaq just above 1,100, down almost 80% from its 2000 peak; the S&P 500 had lost about half its value. Then better-than-expected profit reports from several big companies lifted shares, and the S&P 500 ended October up 9% at 885.76.
imageCaption: The New York Stock Exchange on Wall Street, 2002

headline: The Nasdaq falls 78% below its record, then rebounds
text: On 9 October the Nasdaq closed at 1,114.11, 78% below its March 2000 record; about 5 trillion dollars of market value has been lost since the record. From there it rose 13.5% by the end of October, led by technology shares.

headline: Citigroup's profit holds up; bank shares rally
text: Citigroup reported on 15 October that core income rose 17% to $3.79 billion in the third quarter, with record results in its consumer business. Stocks rallied from the lows they hit early in the month, and Citigroup's shares rose a quarter in October.
imageCaption: Citigroup Center in the Manhattan skyline at night

headline: IBM surprises with growing profits and buys PwC Consulting
text: On 16 October IBM reported third-quarter earnings of 99 cents a share from continuing operations, up from 97 cents, on flat revenue of 19.8 billion dollars, in what it called one of the toughest spending environments it has faced. On 1 October it completed the purchase of PricewaterhouseCoopers' consulting arm for about 3.5 billion dollars. The stock market hit a new low on 9 October and then rallied.
imageCaption: IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, New York

headline: Cisco grows again as tech stocks rebound
text: Cisco reported on November 6 that sales for the quarter to October rose 9% from a year earlier to $4.8 billion, with a profit of $618 million. It holds $21.2 billion in cash and investments. Chambers said Cisco is 'well positioned for an upturn, regardless of when it occurs.' Technology shares have rebounded since early October.
imageCaption: John Chambers on stage at a Cisco event, April 2002
imageCredit: Cisco Systems (Center for Cisco Heritage archive, Computer History Museum)

headline: Nvidia unveils the GeForce FX
text: At the Comdex show in November Nvidia announced the GeForce FX, its new generation of graphics processors, built to compete with ATI's Radeon 9700. The first cards are due early next year. The stock market rose again in November.
imageCaption: The Nvidia GeForce FX 5800 Ultra graphics card

headline: 2002 in review: a third losing year in a row
text: The S&P 500 fell 23% in 2002 to 879.82, its third losing year in a row and its worst of the game so far; it is 40% below where it stood at the end of 1999. The Dow lost 16.8% to 8,341.63. Accounting scandals, the WorldCom and Enron bankruptcies, a weak economy and the threat of war with Iraq weighed on shares, and the Fed cut its key rate to 1.25 percent in November.
imageCaption: The trading floor of the New York Stock Exchange

headline: Greenberg out, Cantalupo back
text: On 5 December McDonald's announced that chairman and chief executive Jack Greenberg will retire at the end of the year. Jim Cantalupo, the former head of McDonald's International who had planned to retire, will succeed him on 1 January, with Charlie Bell, head of McDonald's Europe, as president and Jim Skinner as vice chairman. In October McDonald's launched a US Dollar Menu.
imageCaption: Jim Cantalupo, McDonald's chief executive
imageCredit: McDonald's Corporation (non-free image on English Wikipedia)

headline: Citigroup settles research probe, sets aside $1.3 billion
text: Citigroup reached a settlement in principle with the SEC, the stock exchanges and New York's attorney general over its analysts' research, the allocation of shares in hot share offerings and related practices. It is taking a fourth-quarter charge of $1.5 billion after tax, most of it a $1.3 billion addition to reserves for the settlement and for lawsuits over Enron and research.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012302012169/y67237exv99w1.txt (Citigroup press release, 23 December 2002; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012303004835/y85900exv99w1.txt (28 April 2003; read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Eliot Spitzer, New York's attorney general, whose office led the research probe

headline: A 2.9 billion dollar write-off on SchlumbergerSema
text: On 10 December Schlumberger said it would take after-tax charges of 2.885 billion dollars, mostly writing off goodwill on the Sema purchase, and cut 1,600 jobs at SchlumbergerSema. Its seismic venture WesternGeco is cutting 1,700 jobs and closing its North American land crews. The IT unit will focus on the energy industry.
source: Schlumberger press release of 10 December 2002 (Form 8-K exhibit 99.1), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/87347/000095013002008377/dex991.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/schlumberger-limited (2002 loss) (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: A Schlumberger laboratory in Tyumen, Russia
